question: Which 24 hours does each daily value of 'day d' cover, measured against hourly rain (and, for the river flow, 15-minute flow)?
how_to_read: shift h: the best-matching 24-hour window starts h hours after 00:00 UTC of day d. day_ends_local: the hour of day d, in local standard time, at which that window ends (24:00 UTC + h). The forecast of the project is issued at the end of the river-flow day t: local midnight (river_flow_day).

readings.era5: against ERA5 hourly rain 1980-2014, as measured
readings.merra2: against MERRA-2 hourly rain 2001-2014, as measured
readings.era5_set_to_imerg: against ERA5, shifted so that IMERG falls on its documented UTC day
readings.merra2_set_to_imerg: against MERRA-2, shifted so that IMERG falls on its documented UTC day

made_up_value_against_era5_hourly.known_window: made here from the hourly rain of the 24 hours that END at 12:00 UTC of day d: shift -12 (07:00 Eastern, 06:00 Central standard time of day d)

made_up_value_against_merra2_hourly.known_window: made here from the hourly rain of the 24 hours that END at 12:00 UTC of day d: shift -12 (07:00 Eastern, 06:00 Central standard time of day d)

era_change.how_to_read: Change of the day end from 1980-1995 to 2001-2014 against ERA5, in hours, basin by basin (negative: the day ends earlier in the later years). The window of the daily MERRA-2 value is the UTC day in every year by construction: its change is a drift between the clocks of the two reanalyses, not a move of a window.

era5.product: ERA5 hourly precipitation (models=era5), mm per hour
era5.grid: nearest grid point of the service to the basin centroid (per_basin)

merra2.product: MERRA-2 PRECTOTCORR (Precipitation Corrected), mm per hour
merra2.grid: MERRA-2 cell that holds the basin centroid, 0.5 x 0.625 degrees (results/satellite_data.json)

notes: Method: a daily value of day d is correlated with the hourly reference rain summed over the 24 hours that start h hours after 00:00 UTC of day d, for h from -30 to +30 in steps of 1 h. The curve has a broad top, so the window is placed at its centre: the middle between the two shifts at which the correlation has fallen 0.06 below its best value (centre_shift_h; the best single shift and the readings for drops 0.03 and 0.1 are listed too). The day then ends at 24:00 UTC + h, given in local standard time: UTC-5 for the Eastern basins and UTC-6 for Leaf River, MS (time zones from the USGS site file). 'Day d' is the calendar date written in the product's table.

Self-test of the code (calibration 1): the daily MERRA-2 value served by UTC day against the hourly MERRA-2 rain it is made of. Best shift +0 h (basins +0 to +0), correlation 1.000: the hour stamps and the zero of the shift are right. The direction of the shift is tested with a made-up daily value, the hourly rain of the 24 hours that END at 12:00 UTC of day d (07:00 Eastern standard time, the morning of day d): it is found at shift -12 h against ERA5 and -12 h against MERRA-2 in every basin (calibration.made_up_value_against_<reference>_hourly; the script stops if it is not), so a day that ends before the UTC day comes out as a negative shift and an earlier local hour. The centre-of-curve reading of the self-test curves is +0.5 h (basins +0.2 to +2.0) where 0 is true, and of the made-up morning value -11.7 h (basins -13.3 to -11.3) where -12 is true: where rain falls mostly at one time of day (afternoon storms in Florida) the curve is lopsided and its centre is pushed by up to that much. That is an error of the method itself, and it need not be the same for a product with another day window.

Calibration 2: IMERG is served by UTC day, so its day ends at 19:00 local standard time (18:00 in Leaf River, MS). This check puts the end at 21:01 against ERA5 and 19:46 against MERRA-2: +2.1 h and +1.1 h off. The daily MERRA-2 against ERA5 comes out +1.8 h off. So the hourly references carry timing errors of their own of one to two hours (ERA5 the larger), and no day end below is known better than that.

Four readings are therefore given for every product (day_ends.<product>.median_by_reading): against each hourly reference as measured, and against each reference after shifting it, basin by basin, so that IMERG falls on its documented UTC day. Which of the three clocks (ERA5, MERRA-2, IMERG) is nearest the truth is not known. The headline value of a basin is the mean of its four readings, and the headline of a product is the median basin. The readings do not cover the same years: ERA5 hourly rain is used for 1980-2014, MERRA-2 hourly rain for 2001-2014 (NASA POWER serves it by the hour from 2001 only), and the IMERG shift is measured from 1998 against ERA5 and from 2001 against MERRA-2. Over 2001-2014 alone the ERA5 reading is 09:28 for Daymet and 19:08 for NLDAS (windows.era5.<product>.2001_2014), to be set against the MERRA-2 readings below.

Rain table (Daymet): the value of day d ends at about 09:00 local standard time ON day d (median basin; basins 07:26 to 18:16). The four readings: 10:42 (ERA5 hourly rain 1980-2014), 08:01 (MERRA-2 hourly rain 2001-2014), 08:22 (ERA5, set to IMERG), 07:28 (MERRA-2, set to IMERG). Basins more than 4 hours from the median: Myakka, FL. Against ERA5 the Daymet day ends at 11:59 in 1980-1995, at 09:28 in 2001-2014 and at 09:21 in the test years. That does not show that the Daymet window moved: in the same check the daily MERRA-2 value, whose window is the UTC day in every year by construction, ends at 21:31 in 1980-1995 and at 20:27 in 2001-2014. Basin by basin the day end changes by -1.8 h for Daymet (median; earlier in 11 of 12 basins), by -1.3 h for the daily MERRA-2 (12 of 12) and by -0.7 h for NLDAS (10 of 12; era_change). A product whose window cannot have moved changes too, so this check cannot tell a move of the Daymet window from a drift between the clocks of the references. Single basins change by more (Daymet: -5.0 h to +6.2 h), as a table built from rain gauges whose reading hours change could; the reading hours of the gauges were not checked here. In the test years the basins that do not fit are Little River, NC, Myakka, FL; in Myakka, FL the Daymet day then ends at 22:10 against ERA5 and 19:34 against MERRA-2 - close to the local day, so that basin has little time-stamp gap.

NLDAS rain: the value of day d ends at about 17:30 local standard time on day d (basins 17:03 to 18:20). The four readings: 19:28 (ERA5 hourly rain 1980-2014), 17:15 (MERRA-2 hourly rain 2001-2014), 17:18 (ERA5, set to IMERG), 16:40 (MERRA-2, set to IMERG). Basins more than 4 hours from the median: none. That is the UTC day (19:00) or a little earlier, within the accuracy of the check. The latest single reading of any basin is 20:48: the NLDAS value of the issue day is complete hours before the forecast is issued.

Maurer rain (1980-2008): median basin 02:55 on day d+1, but the basins range from 12:45 to 06:10 on day d+1. Basins more than 4 hours from the median: NE Cape Fear, NC, Catawba, NC, Murder Creek, GA. Maurer has no single day window in these basins, and in the median basin its value of day d reaches past local midnight: the regression below gives the rain of the hours after local midnight a weight of 0.56 in the Maurer value (before 1996, against ERA5; 0.70 for October 2005 to 2008 against MERRA-2). No model of the project reads Maurer rain.

After-midnight rain in the NLDAS value of the issue day (future_rain): the daily value is regressed on the reference rain of six stretches around the day; a weight of 1 means that stretch is fully inside the daily value. Weight of the rain between local midnight and 12:00 UTC of the next day (the first hours after the forecast is issued), median basin: test years 0.00 against MERRA-2 and 0.00 against ERA5 - none. Years before 1996, against ERA5 (NASA POWER serves MERRA-2 by the hour from 2001 only): 0.17. That number is inconclusive, not a leak: in the same regression the daily MERRA-2, which ends at 24:00 UTC by construction, gets 0.19 (test years: 0.13, IMERG 0.08). ERA5 places rain late enough to produce a weight of that size for a product known to hold no such rain. The test years, on which every score of the project rests, are clean; for the training years before 1996 this check can neither show nor exclude a blurred NLDAS day boundary.

The same regression for Daymet, test years against MERRA-2: weight 0.93 for the 12 hours before the UTC day (07:00 to 19:00 Eastern time of day d-1), 1.00 for 19:00 of day d-1 to 07:00 of day d, and 0.22 for 07:00 to 19:00 of day d: most of the daytime rain of day d is not in the Daymet value of day d.

River flow: 15-minute flow of 12 of the 12 gauges (USGS, 2012-01-05 to 2012-06-25) averaged over 24-hour windows shifted hour by hour and compared with the daily flow in the CAMELS files, every window on the same days; the best window is the one with the smallest mean relative difference. While standard time is in force (2012-01-05 to 2012-03-09) the window from local midnight to midnight is the best one in 12 of 12 gauges (median difference 0.30% of the daily flow, against 3.77% for the UTC day). While daylight-saving time is in force (2012-03-13 to 2012-06-25) the best window is midnight to midnight by the summer clock - one hour earlier in standard time - in 10 gauges, and standard-time midnight in 2 (Murder Creek, GA, Turkey Creek, GA); median difference 0.46% by the summer clock, 0.78% by standard time, 3.41% for the UTC day. So a daily flow value is the mean from midnight to midnight by the local clock, not the UTC day: 'the end of day t', when a forecast is issued, is local midnight - in summer, at most gauges, 23:00 on the standard-time axis used in this file and in the figure. French Broad, NC, over the whole period, as the reviewer of 10_rain_timing.py measured it: RMSE 1.51 cfs for standard-time midnight, 3.17 cfs for summer-time midnight and 18.12 cfs for the UTC day (mean flow 226 cfs). Six months of one year were checked, not the whole record.

Summer time and the rain checks: all rain windows are given in standard time, and the regression counts rain as 'after the forecast' from standard-time midnight on. In summer the flow day of most gauges ends one hour earlier, so the last hour before standard-time midnight is then also after the forecast. That hour lies in the stretch 'evening until local midnight', whose weight in the NLDAS value of the test years is 0.04 against MERRA-2 and 0.14 against ERA5 (the daily MERRA-2, which holds none of that rain by construction, gets 0.29 against ERA5).

Limits. (1) Both references are reanalyses: their rain is computed by a weather model that is corrected with observations, and its hour-by-hour timing is less sure than its daily total; calibration 2 puts a number on that. (2) The references are values of one grid cell at the basin centroid (ERA5: the grid points returned lie on a 0.25 degree grid, up to 0.12 degrees from the centroid; MERRA-2: 0.5 x 0.625 degrees), the daily products are basin averages (IMERG: its 0.1 degree cells weighted by area); a storm can reach the cell and the basin at different hours. (3) The method finds the ONE 24-hour window that fits best. A table built from stations that are read at different hours is a mix of windows: its curve is broad, and the centre is an average, not a sharp boundary - so 'ends at about 09:00' does not mean that no later rain is inside. (4) A shifted window cannot be told from a product whose rain is smeared in time, nor from a timing error of the reference. (5) Hours are standard time; the shifts are whole hours. (6) Correlations are dominated by the large storms.

Sources. ERA5 hourly precipitation: Open-Meteo historical weather API (archive-api.open-meteo.com, models=era5, timezone UTC), 1980-09-25 to 2014-10-05, one request per basin centroid; the service returns the grid point it used (sources.era5.per_basin). Its value at time T is taken as the rain of the hour before T, as the service documents it; if that were the hour after, every ERA5 reading would move by one hour. MERRA-2 hourly: NASA POWER hourly point API, parameter PRECTOTCORR ('Precipitation Corrected', mm/hour), time standard UTC, 2001-01-01 to 2014-10-05. USGS: instantaneous-values service (waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/iv, parameter 00060, discharge) and site file. Retrieval dates are the dates of the cached files in data/hourly.

Fair test: nothing is trained, chosen or tuned here, and no forecast is scored. The check describes the input data over the whole record; the eras (before 1996, 2001-2014, the test years) are reported side by side.
